title: Precursor-to-Scheming Predictivity: A Cheap Replication of Apollo's Null Result

original_idea.body:
# Precursor-to-Scheming Predictivity: A Cheap Replication of Apollo's Null Result

**Problem:** Apollo reported that their scheming PRECURSOR evals (self-reasoning, theory-of-mind) had limited predictive power for actual in-context scheming — a broken link in the assumed chain precursor-capability -> scheming-behavior. This surprising negative result is rarely replicated independently on open models.

**Direction:** Assemble a small set of public precursor-style tasks (agentic self-reasoning, applied theory-of-mind) and a small set of toy scheming tasks (oversight evasion, goal-guarding). Across several open models, correlate precursor scores with scheming-action rates to test whether the predictive link is weak, as Apollo found. Report the correlation and its uncertainty.

**Why it matters:** Safety cases lean on precursor evals as early-warning tripwires; independently confirming (or refuting) their weak predictivity is high-value for the field and requires only inference on open models.

**Relevant context:** Apollo 'Research Note: Our scheming precursor evals had limited predictive power for our in-context scheming evals'; precursor evals split into self-reasoning and applied theory-of-mind.
